metadata.narrative: I work for a New York City council member whose district has a lot of transit riders but also some small businesses worried about delivery costs. Can you help me understand whether congestion pricing is a credible and fair way to fund the MTA? What should we weigh about the revenue promise, who pays, who benefits, environmental tradeoffs in places like the Bronx and New Jersey, and whether the MTA and Albany can be held accountable for actually spending the money on reliable service instead of repeating past mistakes?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Congestion pricing in New York City is formally the Central Business District Tolling Program, a fee charged to most vehicles entering Manhattan south of 60th Street that is meant to both thin traffic and generate dedicated new revenue for the MTA's capital program.

The revenue promise is grounded in real modeling: the MTA's environmental assessment laid out toll scenarios from $9 to $23 at peak hours and projected the program would raise roughly $1 billion a year, enough to support about $15 billion in bonded capital investment for subway and bus modernization.
Under the enacted plan, that money is split so about 80 percent goes to the subway and bus network and roughly 10 percent to commuter railroads, giving the promise a specific, checkable target.

On who pays, MTA data show the toll falls overwhelmingly on a narrow slice of higher-income drivers rather than typical transit riders: 85 percent of existing trips into the district are already made by transit, with only about 5 percent by car from the city, 3 percent from suburban counties, and 3 percent from New Jersey.

In one transit-dependent Brooklyn district, only about 6 percent of commuters into the zone drive at all, just 1.9 percent would pay the toll, and those drivers earn on average $10,000 more per year than transit riders.
Citywide, fewer than 5,000 low-income outer-borough residents commute into the zone by car, compared with 190,000 who use the subway, which is the core of the "who benefits" case.

The program layers discounts on top of that: residents inside the zone earning under $60,000 get a credit, taxi and for-hire drivers earning under $50,000 get a 25 percent discount after ten monthly trips, and trucks get a 50 percent overnight discount.
Your small-business concern deserves a direct answer: one delivery-service owner told reporters the toll would force him to raise prices.

Advocates counter that less gridlock lets delivery drivers and tradespeople complete more stops per day, potentially offsetting the toll, though this "more stops" math is not independently verified for every trade.
That tension — real short-term cost pass-through versus theoretical productivity gains — is worth flagging honestly rather than resolving with false certainty.
The environmental picture is genuinely mixed, and the South Bronx is the clearest example of an unresolved equity cost.

The MTA's own Environmental Assessment found that in every one of seven tolling scenarios studied, the South Bronx would see increased air pollution as trucks divert around the tolled zone, even as three other boroughs would see improvement.

Independent research from Columbia's Mailman School and South Bronx Unite documented worsening congestion in Mott Haven and Port Morris between 2017 and 2019, tied to a 17 percent childhood asthma rate and pedestrian injury rates nearly double the citywide average.

The Biden administration's HHS flagged this before implementation, warning the MTA that all tolling scenarios would increase heavy-truck trips along the Cross Bronx Expressway, a corridor that already breathes more diesel particulate than 98 percent of U.S. communities.

Officials committed to mitigation — an asthma center, $20 million for asthma programs, $10 million for school air filtration, and greener freight facilities at Hunts Point — but those commitments are tied to the program continuing, so losing the toll also means losing that mitigation funding.

New Jersey's objection is different: after federal approval, officials including Senator Menendez and Representatives Gottheimer and Pascrell demanded exemptions for tunnel and bridge drivers, arguing New York was balancing its budget on New Jersey commuters, while clean-energy groups filed counter-briefs supporting the toll.
Accountability is where the promise is most fragile, and your office should press hard here.

Congestion pricing revenue is bonded specifically for the capital plan; by design none flows into the MTA's operating budget, so it cannot by itself fix service reliability or maintenance backlogs funded differently.

New York's "lockbox" law only prevents money from being diverted away from the MTA — it does not guarantee any particular level of new spending, and MTA operating costs per service-hour have risen faster than inflation for years.

History reinforces that caution: Albany has previously withheld or redirected dedicated MTA tax revenue during budget disputes, and Governor Cuomo once pledged $8.3 billion in capital support that ultimately delivered only about $805 million through a "last-dollar-in" structure that delays real accountability.

Concrete overrun examples exist too, such as a roughly $400 million MTA office renovation that ran $170 million over budget with limited public explanation, and watchdogs like Reinvent Albany have found MTA capital plans lack year-by-year transparency even as debt service already consumes about 16 percent of the operating budget.

The program's political fragility compounds the financial risk: Governor Hochul abruptly and indefinitely paused the fully built tolling infrastructure in June 2024 just weeks before launch, a move the Regional Plan Association called "a betrayal of millions of transit riders," and the Trump administration separately stalled federal environmental review for years with hundreds of follow-up questions before eventually approving it.

Taken together, congestion pricing is a credible funding mechanism with real modeling behind its revenue targets and a defensible fairness case, since the toll concentrates costs on a wealthier minority of drivers while directing benefits to the much larger population of transit riders, and includes real, if imperfect, discounts for low-income drivers, taxis, and overnight trucking.

Its fairness case is weakened, however, by a concentrated and only partially mitigated pollution burden on the South Bronx, contested cost-shifting concerns from New Jersey and some small delivery operators, and a genuine accountability gap in which lockbox protections, bonding structures, and Albany's own funding record fall short of guaranteeing that the money reaches riders as reliable service rather than repeating past capital-plan shortfalls.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

query.description: A natural-language query for evidence relevant to the research request.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

budget_tokens_per_result.description: Maximum approximate tokens staged per result. Text is bounded at tokens × 5 characters and cut at the final line break before that boundary. Default 4096.

tools.name: commit_context

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

reason.description: The distinct evidence, claim, perspective, date, name, counter-evidence, or coverage area this document uniquely contributes.

The revenue promise itself is grounded in real modeling rather than guesswork: the MTA's own environmental assessment laid out toll scenarios ranging from $9 to $23 at peak hours and projected the program would raise roughly $1 billion a year, enough to support about $15 billion in bonded capital investment for subway and bus modernization.

Citywide comparisons found fewer than 5,000 low-income outer-borough residents commute into the zone by car, compared with 190,000 who use the subway, which is the core of the "who benefits" case: far more low-income New Yorkers ride transit than drive into Manhattan.

The program layers real discounts on top of that base fairness case: residents inside the zone earning under $60,000 get a credit, taxi and for-hire drivers earning under $50,000 get a 25 percent discount after ten monthly trips, and trucks receive a 50 percent overnight discount to shift freight to off-peak hours.

Your small-business and delivery concern deserves a direct, unvarnished answer: some operators say the toll will simply be passed to customers, as one delivery-service owner told reporters it would force him to raise prices.
[shard_04242_60010]

[shard_01687_61142] [shard_04125_66359] [shard_04472_66929]

Taken together, congestion pricing is a credible funding mechanism with real modeling behind its revenue targets and a defensible fairness case, since the toll concentrates costs on a wealthier minority of drivers while directing benefits to the much larger population of transit riders and includes real, if imperfect, discounts for low-income drivers, taxis, and overnight trucking.

answer.text: Congestion pricing in New York City is formally the Central Business District Tolling Program, a fee charged to most vehicles entering Manhattan south of 60th Street that is meant to both thin traffic and generate dedicated new revenue for the MTA's capital program.

The revenue promise is grounded in real modeling: the MTA's environmental assessment laid out toll scenarios from $9 to $23 at peak hours and projected the program would raise roughly $1 billion a year, enough to support about $15 billion in bonded capital investment for subway and bus modernization.
Under the enacted plan, that money is split so about 80 percent goes to the subway and bus network and roughly 10 percent to commuter railroads, giving the promise a specific, checkable target.

On who pays, MTA data show the toll falls overwhelmingly on a narrow slice of higher-income drivers rather than typical transit riders: 85 percent of existing trips into the district are already made by transit, with only about 5 percent by car from the city, 3 percent from suburban counties, and 3 percent from New Jersey.

In one transit-dependent Brooklyn district, only about 6 percent of commuters into the zone drive at all, just 1.9 percent would pay the toll, and those drivers earn on average $10,000 more per year than transit riders.
Citywide, fewer than 5,000 low-income outer-borough residents commute into the zone by car, compared with 190,000 who use the subway, which is the core of the "who benefits" case.

The program layers discounts on top of that: residents inside the zone earning under $60,000 get a credit, taxi and for-hire drivers earning under $50,000 get a 25 percent discount after ten monthly trips, and trucks get a 50 percent overnight discount.
Your small-business concern deserves a direct answer: one delivery-service owner told reporters the toll would force him to raise prices.

Advocates counter that less gridlock lets delivery drivers and tradespeople complete more stops per day, potentially offsetting the toll, though this "more stops" math is not independently verified for every trade.
That tension — real short-term cost pass-through versus theoretical productivity gains — is worth flagging honestly rather than resolving with false certainty.
The environmental picture is genuinely mixed, and the South Bronx is the clearest example of an unresolved equity cost.

The MTA's own Environmental Assessment found that in every one of seven tolling scenarios studied, the South Bronx would see increased air pollution as trucks divert around the tolled zone, even as three other boroughs would see improvement.

Independent research from Columbia's Mailman School and South Bronx Unite documented worsening congestion in Mott Haven and Port Morris between 2017 and 2019, tied to a 17 percent childhood asthma rate and pedestrian injury rates nearly double the citywide average.

The Biden administration's HHS flagged this before implementation, warning the MTA that all tolling scenarios would increase heavy-truck trips along the Cross Bronx Expressway, a corridor that already breathes more diesel particulate than 98 percent of U.S. communities.

Officials committed to mitigation — an asthma center, $20 million for asthma programs, $10 million for school air filtration, and greener freight facilities at Hunts Point — but those commitments are tied to the program continuing, so losing the toll also means losing that mitigation funding.

New Jersey's objection is different: after federal approval, officials including Senator Menendez and Representatives Gottheimer and Pascrell demanded exemptions for tunnel and bridge drivers, arguing New York was balancing its budget on New Jersey commuters, while clean-energy groups filed counter-briefs supporting the toll.
Accountability is where the promise is most fragile, and your office should press hard here.

Congestion pricing revenue is bonded specifically for the capital plan; by design none flows into the MTA's operating budget, so it cannot by itself fix service reliability or maintenance backlogs funded differently.

New York's "lockbox" law only prevents money from being diverted away from the MTA — it does not guarantee any particular level of new spending, and MTA operating costs per service-hour have risen faster than inflation for years.

History reinforces that caution: Albany has previously withheld or redirected dedicated MTA tax revenue during budget disputes, and Governor Cuomo once pledged $8.3 billion in capital support that ultimately delivered only about $805 million through a "last-dollar-in" structure that delays real accountability.

Concrete overrun examples exist too, such as a roughly $400 million MTA office renovation that ran $170 million over budget with limited public explanation, and watchdogs like Reinvent Albany have found MTA capital plans lack year-by-year transparency even as debt service already consumes about 16 percent of the operating budget.

The program's political fragility compounds the financial risk: Governor Hochul abruptly and indefinitely paused the fully built tolling infrastructure in June 2024 just weeks before launch, a move the Regional Plan Association called "a betrayal of millions of transit riders," and the Trump administration separately stalled federal environmental review for years with hundreds of follow-up questions before eventually approving it.

Taken together, congestion pricing is a credible funding mechanism with real modeling behind its revenue targets and a defensible fairness case, since the toll concentrates costs on a wealthier minority of drivers while directing benefits to the much larger population of transit riders, and includes real, if imperfect, discounts for low-income drivers, taxis, and overnight trucking.

Its fairness case is weakened, however, by a concentrated and only partially mitigated pollution burden on the South Bronx, contested cost-shifting concerns from New Jersey and some small delivery operators, and a genuine accountability gap in which lockbox protections, bonding structures, and Albany's own funding record fall short of guaranteeing that the money reaches riders as reliable service rather than repeating past capital-plan shortfalls.
